Then the ringmaster gave a short speech. He said he hoped there would be no disturbance, and if the man promised to stop making trouble, he could ride, provided he thought he could stay on the horse. Everybody laughed and agreed, and the man climbed up. The instant he was aboard, the horse started bucking and leaping and tearing around. Two circus men clung to its bridle, trying to hold it, while the drunk hugged its neck, his heels flying up at every jump. The whole audience stood shouting and laughing until tears ran down their faces. Finally, despite everything the circus men could do, the horse broke free and went racing around and around the ring like mad. The drunk lay along its back, gripping its neck, with one leg dangling almost to the ground on one side, then the other leg on the other side, while the crowd went wild. I couldn’t find it funny. I was trembling all over at the danger he was in. But before long he struggled into a proper seat and caught the bridle, swaying back and forth. Then, the very next moment, he sprang up, let go of the bridle, and stood on the horse, which was still running at a furious speed! He stayed up there, sailing around as comfortably as if he had never been drunk in his life. Then he began stripping off clothes and flinging them away. They came off so fast they almost filled the air. Altogether he took off seventeen suits. And there he was, slim and handsome, wearing the brightest, prettiest outfit you ever saw. He laid into the horse with his whip and really made it fly. At last he jumped off, bowed, and danced away to the dressing room, with everyone howling in delight and amazement.

Then the ringmaster realized he’d been fooled, and I reckon you never saw a more embarrassed ringmaster. Why, the fellow was one of his own performers! He had dreamed up the whole joke himself and hadn’t told a soul. I felt foolish enough at being taken in, but I wouldn’t have traded places with that ringmaster for a thousand dollars. Maybe there are better circuses than that one; I don’t know, because I’ve never come across them. Anyway, it was more than good enough for me. Whenever I run into it again, it can count on getting all my business.

“Next, we put up a wire fence.”

“A wire fence?”

“Yes. You suggested it yourself two or three years ago.”

“Oh, I remember. That was when the Church first tested its strength against us, then decided to wait for a better opportunity. Well, how have you set up the fence?”

“Twelve very strong wires, bare and without insulation, run from a large generator in the cave. It has only two brushes, one positive and one negative—”

“Yes, that’s right.”

“The wires leave the cave and enclose a flat circular area a hundred yards across. They form twelve separate fences, ten feet apart: twelve circles, one inside another. Their ends run back into the cave.”

“Good. Go on.”

“The fences are secured to heavy oak posts only three feet apart, buried five feet deep.”

“That sounds strong enough.”

“Yes. None of the wires is connected to the ground outside the cave. They leave the generator’s positive brush, and the negative brush connects to the ground. The far ends of the wires return to the cave, where each has its own ground connection.”

“No, no, that won’t work!”

“Why not?”

“It costs too much. You’re wasting power. The only ground connection you need is through the negative brush. Bring the other end of each wire back into the cave and fasten it separately, without connecting it to the ground. Now see how that saves energy. Suppose cavalry charges the fence. Until the horses hit the wires, you use no power and spend no money, because there is only one ground connection. The instant the horses touch a wire, they connect it to the negative brush through the earth, and they fall dead. Do you see? You use energy only when you need it. Your lightning waits ready, like a loaded gun, without costing a penny until you fire. Yes, that single ground connection—”

“Of course! How did I miss that? It’s cheaper and works better too. If wires break or get tangled, it does no harm.”

“No, especially if we have an indicator in the cave and disconnect any broken wire. Now, go on. What about the Gatling guns?”

“Yes, those are ready. In the middle of the innermost circle, on a roomy platform six feet high, I’ve set up thirteen Gatling guns, with plenty of ammunition.”

“Excellent. They cover every approach. When the Church’s knights arrive, there’ll be music. And the cliff edge above the cave—”

“I’ve put a wire fence and a Gatling gun there.”

“Perhaps the hardest part of this adventure to explain was my own stunned surprise at the extraordinary change in my position. The turning over itself was natural and unavoidable. Indeed, I had long expected it to happen when I reached the point in my journey where the moon’s pull became stronger than the earth’s—or, more exactly, where gravity pulled the balloon toward the moon more strongly than toward the earth. Admittedly, I had awakened from deep sleep with my senses confused, only to face a startling sight. Although I had expected it eventually, I had not expected it at that moment. The turning must have happened gently and gradually. Even if I had been awake, I might not have noticed any sign of it inside the balloon. Nothing about my own position or my equipment need have shifted or caused any discomfort.

“Once I understood where I was and recovered from the terror that had taken hold of my whole mind, I naturally turned all my attention to the moon’s general appearance. It spread beneath me like a map. I believed it was still a considerable distance away, yet I could see the hollows of its surface with a clarity that was both remarkable and entirely unexplained. At first glance, its strangest physical feature was the complete lack of oceans or seas. There were no lakes, rivers, or other bodies of water either. Oddly enough, however, I saw enormous flat regions that clearly looked as though they had been formed from material deposited by water. Most of the visible half of the moon, though, was covered in countless cone-shaped volcanic mountains. They looked more like structures someone had built than natural features. The tallest rises no more than three and three-quarter miles straight up. But a map of the volcanic areas of the Campi Phlegraei would give Your Excellencies a better idea of their general appearance than any poor description I could attempt. Most of these volcanoes were plainly erupting. Their fury and power became frighteningly clear to me through the repeated thunder of the stones wrongly called meteoric. These now rushed upward past the balloon with a frequency that grew more terrifying by the moment.”
